Chapter Six: The War That Changed Everything
The summer of 1914 rolled in with this heavy sense of unease. But honestly, almost no one could have guessed just how fast the world was about to unravel. For the three royal cousins—George, Nicholas, and Wilhelm—the outbreak of war wasn’t just a political crisis. It was deeply personal. Everything that once connected them—those handwritten letters, family gatherings, even the little rituals and inside jokes—were suddenly swept away by the chaos of total war.
Each of them was forced to face an uncomfortable truth: the choices they’d made, all those moments of hesitation or pride, had helped push Europe right to the edge.
Wilhelm, who’d always wanted to prove himself, suddenly found the responsibility of command almost too much to bear. The German war machine, once set in motion by the country’s generals and ministers, seemed unstoppable—and strangely indifferent to the man at the top. Wilhelm tried to steer events, pacing the halls of his palace, reading endless reports, issuing orders. But the real decisions? Those were happening somewhere else. The Kaiser’s bluster faded, replaced by gnawing anxiety and regret. He watched as Germany became isolated, his own people suffering, and the armies locked in a brutal struggle on two fronts. The respect he’d longed for from Britain and Russia? Now, it was replaced by hatred and fear.
Nicholas, the Tsar of Russia, felt just as overwhelmed. The Russian army was enormous, but plagued by poor leadership and disastrous losses. Nicholas’s belief in his divine right to rule—something he’d held onto all his life—was deeply shaken by the scale of the disaster. At home, the strains of war only made Russia’s divisions worse. Food became scarce, strikes and protests happened every day. Nicholas clung to his family for comfort, trying to lose himself in the routines of palace life, but the outside world was changing too quickly for him to keep up. His wife, Alexandra, grew more influential, turning to mystics and advisers who claimed they could save Russia, but only brought more confusion. The Tsar became more and more isolated, and with that, less able to respond to the crisis around him.
Over in Britain, George faced his own kind of challenge. The war called for unity and sacrifice, and suddenly, the monarchy became a symbol of national strength and resolve. George threw himself into the role: visiting hospitals, inspecting troops, doing whatever he could to keep people’s spirits up. He knew that if the monarchy was going to survive, it had to adapt, to become part of the nation’s struggle—not just stand apart from it. The British royal family even changed its name—from the very German-sounding Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to the House of Windsor—to put some distance between themselves and the enemy. George’s steady presence reassured people, but he couldn’t shake the fact that his own cousins now stood on the other side of the conflict.
And so the war dragged on, year after year, costing millions of lives. The old world, with all its traditions and certainties, was being destroyed in the trenches of the Western Front and across the fields of Eastern Europe. The cousins, who once shared family ties and so much history, were now divided by suspicion, hatred, and the relentless demands of war. Letters stopped. Old photographs faded. The bonds of kinship, built carefully over generations, simply broke apart.
Most of us don’t realize just how quickly the familiar can become strange—or how easily love can turn to enmity. This war didn’t just redraw the map of Europe. It changed the hearts and minds of everyone who lived through it. For George, Nicholas, and Wilhelm, the world they’d inherited was gone for good. And nothing—no matter how hard they tried—could bring it back.
